title: Reproducibility and provenance: hashing graphs and seeds

questions.q: According to the lesson, why is saving the random seed alone considered a dangerous misconception for reproducibility?
options: Because seeds are randomly generated and cannot be stored.
Because if the lock (node version, operation order, or precision) changes, the key (seed) will not open the same door.
Because seeds only work with specific hardware configurations.
Because seeds are not part of the cryptographic hash function.
questions.answer: Because if the lock (node version, operation order, or precision) changes, the key (seed) will not open the same door.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'A seed is merely a key to a lock; if the lock itself changes—due to a different node version, a different order of operations, or a floating-point precision shift—the key will not open the same door.'

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'canonicalization' in the context of hashing a workflow graph?
options: To compress the graph size for faster transmission.
To convert the graph into a single, unambiguous string by sorting keys and standardizing format.
To encrypt the graph so only authorized users can view it.
To remove all seed values from the graph structure.
questions.answer: To convert the graph into a single, unambiguous string by sorting keys and standardizing format.
questions.why: The lesson explains: 'To prove that two workflows are identical... we must convert them into a single, unambiguous string of text. This is called canonicalization. By sorting the keys and standardizing the format, we remove ambiguity.'

questions.q: In the provided lab example, what does the output line 'RESULT tensor_op = 2' prove?
options: That the SHA-256 hash was calculated correctly.
That the PyTorch environment is deterministic and floating-point operations yield consistent results.
That the KSampler node was successfully initialized.
That the server history was retrieved without errors.
questions.answer: That the PyTorch environment is deterministic and floating-point operations yield consistent results.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'This line confirms that the PyTorch environment is deterministic. The operation tensor * 2.0 on a float32 tensor yields exactly 2.0. If this value varied between runs, our entire reproducibility framework would be compromised by floating-point non-determinism.'

questions.q: What specific parameter must be set to True during JSON serialization to ensure that identical graphs produce identical hashes, and why?
questions.answer: sort_keys=True, because without it, the order of keys in the JSON may vary depending on the Python version or dictionary construction order, leading to different hashes for identical graphs.
questions.why: The lesson lists 'Non-canonical serialization' as a common mistake: 'If you serialize the graph without sorting keys, the order of keys in the JSON may vary... This will lead to different hashes for identical graphs. Always use sort_keys=True.'

questions.q: According to the 'Common mistakes' section, what is the risk of assuming the server state is immutable when verifying provenance?
options: The server will delete the history after 24 hours.
If you modify the graph after execution, the hash of the current graph will not match the hash of the executed graph.
The get_history function will return a null value.
The cryptographic hash function will fail to compute.
questions.answer: If you modify the graph after execution, the hash of the current graph will not match the hash of the executed graph.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'If you modify the graph after execution, the hash of the current graph will not match the hash of the executed graph. Always hash the prompt as it was sent.'
